prompt: What inspections are required during construction in Toronto?
answer:
The required inspections depend on whether your project is classified as a small building (Part 9) or large building (Part 3) under the Ontario Building Code.

For large buildings (Part 3), required inspections include:

**Building Inspections:**
- Footings (at completion of formwork, before pouring concrete)
- Foundations (at completion)
- Structural framing (at completion of structural framing for each storey)
- Fire separations and closures (at completion of framing for wall, floor and shaft fire separations)
- Insulation and vapour/air barrier (at completion and before interior services)
- Fireplaces, gas appliances, and chimneys (at commencement of installation)
- Life safety systems (at completion of rough-in)
- Final interior inspection (at completion of interior construction)
- Final exterior inspection (at completion of grading and exterior finishes)

**Plumbing Inspections:**
- Site meeting (at start of construction)
- Outside storm & sanitary sewers (at completion, before backfilling)
- Water service (at completion, before backfilling)
- Inside storm & sanitary sewers (at completion)
- Rough-in, water supply, drains, waste & vents (at completion)
- Final inspection (at completion of all fixtures)

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/when-to-call-for-inspection-of-large-buildings/]

For small buildings (houses and small commercial structures under Part 9), the specific inspection requirements are not detailed in the provided evidence. A Building Inspector can assist you in confirming which inspections are required for your particular project. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]

prompt: What is an express building permit and do I qualify?

**Small Residential Projects:**
- Part 9 houses with not more than two dwelling units (no active permits for new buildings/additions)
- Detached ancillary structures (garages, carports, sheds)
- Decks and porches
- Interior alterations
- Basement walkouts and underpinning
- Work impacting party walls (with enhanced requirements)
- Minor fire damage repair
- 1 to 2 unit conversions (max 2 units per building)
- Stand-alone plumbing and drain permits
- Solar panel installations attached to existing buildings

**Small Commercial Projects:**
- Interior alterations to Assembly/Industrial occupancies (up to 300 m², no change in use/patron area)
- Interior alterations to Business/Office/Retail/Restaurants with <30 seats (up to 600 m², no change in use/patron area)
- Tents (including certified tents)
- Minor fire damage repair
- Stand-alone maglocks
- Solar panel installations

**Sign Permits:**
- First party signs (up to 3 signs)
- Third party signs (up to 3 signs)

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

To determine if you specifically qualify, I would need to know what type of project you're planning (residential/commercial, specific work type, size, etc.).

prompt: What are the requirements for a laneway suite permit?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, here are the key requirements for a laneway suite building permit:

**General Requirements:**
- Must be a self-contained residential unit on the same lot as a detached house, semi-detached house, or townhouse, generally located in the rear yard next to a laneway [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]
- All drawings must be on standardized sized sheets, drawn to scale, fully dimensioned, signed and dated [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]
- If prepared by a qualified designer, drawings must include the designer's name, registration number, qualification identification number, signature, and stamp/statement [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]
- All documents must be provided in PDF format [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

**Fire Access Requirements:**
- Must provide a level, unobstructed exterior path for firefighters no longer than 45 metres in length [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2020/ph/bgrd/backgroundfile-156421.pdf]
- Minimum dimensions of 1.0 metre-wide by 2.1 metres-high for the fire access path [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2020/ph/bgrd/backgroundfile-156421.pdf]
- Access must be provided from the street that the existing house faces or from a flanking street that accesses the end of the public laneway [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]
- Where the 1.0 metre-wide path cannot be provided on the subject property, it may be shared with a neighboring property through a Limiting Distance Agreement [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2020/ph/bgrd/backgroundfile-156421.pdf]

**Additional Considerations:**
- Must protect any healthy trees on the property [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]
- Must provide principal access as per Ontario Building Code Division B 9.9.2.4 and fire access as per Division B 9.10.20.3 [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

prompt: What happens if I build without a permit in Toronto?
answer:
If you build without a permit in Toronto, you could face serious and potentially costly consequences [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/98ad-Good_Neighbour_Guide_Digital-shrunk.pdf]. These include:

*   **Administrative Fees:** You will be charged a "work without permit" fee equal to 50 percent of the permit fees for the project. This fee has a minimum and maximum value that is updated periodically [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
*   **Work Stoppage:** All work must stop while your permit application is processed, which will cause delays [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
*   **Correction of Work:** You may have to undo work that has already been done or perform additional work (such as structural or mechanical upgrades) that was not originally planned or budgeted for [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
*   **Legal and Financial Issues:** You may encounter legal or financial problems later, such as difficulties selling your property or making insurance claims [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
*   **Enforcement Measures:** Property owners who fail to comply may face progressive enforcement measures, including legal action [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/closing-building-permits/].

Even if you hired a contractor who said a permit was not needed, you, as the homeowner, are responsible for paying these fees and penalties [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
